blocks.title: Trace state one instruction at a time
paragraphs: Assembly exposes operations on architectural state: registers, memory and the next instruction. In AT&T syntax the source normally comes before the destination. Record the state before a step, evaluate its operands, then apply the documented update.

The existing Visualizer executes a deliberately limited 64-bit subset. This lesson also explains register widths for reading real x86-64 code; byte/word/dword examples are explicitly non-executable in that tool.

blocks.title: Distinguish a value, an address and a memory read
paragraphs: In movq $9, %rax, the dollar sign makes 9 an immediate value; RAX becomes 9. In movq %rax, -8(%rbp), the value is stored at address RBP−8. In leaq -8(%rbp), %rax, the address itself is written to RAX without reading that memory cell.
For RBP=0x1000, the effective address RBP−8 is 0x0FF8. If memory there holds 9, movq -8(%rbp), %rax loads 9, while leaq -8(%rbp), %rax yields 4088. The q suffix denotes an eight-byte operation.

blocks.title: Partial-register writes have different effects
paragraphs: Reading-only example, outside the Visualizer subset: start with RAX=0x1122334455667788. Writing AL=0xAA replaces the low byte, giving 0x11223344556677AA. Writing AX=0xBBBB instead replaces the low word, giving 0x112233445566BBBB.

Writing EAX=0x12345678 clears the upper 32 bits of RAX, giving 0x0000000012345678. A 64-bit RAX write replaces the entire register. These cases are independent writes from the stated original value; do not carry one example into the next.

blocks.title: Build and unwind a stack frame
paragraphs: The stack grows toward lower addresses. Starting at RSP=RBP=0x1000, pushq %rbp moves RSP to 0x0FF8 and stores the prior RBP there. movq %rsp, %rbp makes 0x0FF8 the stable frame base; subq $16, %rsp reserves space down to 0x0FE8.

Locations -8(%rbp) and -16(%rbp) are then 0x0FF0 and 0x0FE8. Restoring RSP from RBP releases those locals, and popq %rbp reads the saved frame pointer and returns RSP to 0x1000. Reserved memory is not automatically initialized.

blocks.title: A call adds a return point to the stack
paragraphs: A call pushes the location to continue at and transfers control. In the Visualizer that location is a zero-based instruction index; real machine code uses an instruction address. ret takes the return location from the stack and resumes there.

For nested calls, track a separate return entry and saved frame for each active invocation. Unwind in reverse order. A function result in RAX does not by itself restore RSP or RBP; the epilogue must preserve the stack contract.

Open the existing Function call example to trace main passing RDI=5, the helper adding 2, and the caller receiving 7 in RAX. The helper is placed before main to avoid unsupported jump/fall-through control.

blocks.title: Debug by checking invariants
paragraphs: Before each read, identify the exact address, width and whether it has been initialized. Before ret, check that the top of the stack is the intended return entry, not a local value or a saved frame pointer.

Compare stack allocation with deallocation along each path, and distinguish caller state from current frame state. Alignment constraints come from the specified calling convention: the Visualizer checks aligned eight-byte words but does not enforce a complete ABI.
Do not paste unsupported partial-register operations into the tool and assume it emulates them. Read its supported-instruction list; use the lesson’s separate reference cases for width semantics.

blocks.title: Keep an exact state ledger
paragraphs: Annotate source and destination, widths, effective addresses, current RSP/RBP and return entries. Compare each post-state with the instruction semantics, then unwind frames in reverse order.
Use Flashcards for distinctions, Practice for partial-register reading and debugging criteria, and the unchanged Assembly Visualizer for executable 64-bit traces.

cards.prompt: What is the usual AT&T operand order?
cards.answer: Source, then destination. An immediate has $, a register has %, and displacement(base) describes a memory effective address.

cards.prompt: How do movq displacement(%rbp), %rax and leaq differ?
cards.answer: movq reads the value stored at the effective address. leaq computes the address itself and does not read memory.

cards.prompt: What happens to the upper half of RAX when EAX is written?
cards.answer: A 32-bit EAX write clears the upper 32 bits of RAX. This reading example is outside the Visualizer’s qword-only subset.

cards.prompt: Do AL and AX writes clear the rest of RAX?
cards.answer: No. They replace the low byte or low word while preserving other bits. A full RAX write replaces all 64 bits.

cards.prompt: What must be at the stack top before ret?
cards.answer: The intended return location. Locals and saved frame values must be unwound first. The tool uses instruction indices for return locations.

cards.prompt: Why is RBP useful after reserving stack locals?
cards.answer: It can remain a stable frame base while RSP moves. This convention only works if the prologue establishes it and the epilogue restores the caller’s state.

cards.prompt: Which invariants help find a broken function epilogue?
cards.answer: Check the exact top-of-stack role, balanced allocation/deallocation, restored saved registers and the stated alignment contract before returning.

guided.title: Diagnose an unbalanced return
guided.prompt: A function saves RBP, sets its frame base, reserves 16 bytes, then immediately executes popq %rbp; ret. Explain the problem and a valid repair.
rubric: RSP still points at reserved local space, so the pop does not read the saved frame pointer.
Restore RSP from the frame base (or undo the exact allocation), then pop the saved RBP, then return.
Trace the return entry separately. Use the supported Stack frame/Function call examples to verify the sequence; no free-form code grade is assigned.
